Why do some brands live for decades?

admin 21 November 2017

Some commercial logos disappear, others live for centuries. So what makes us love or offer a slogan? Sometime in 1855, an unknown genius sat down to design a motto. It was a simple crimson triangle, but it continued and spread throughout the world. The logo was pasted on bottles of the famous 'Bass Bell' beer, a beer that tastes like barley. In the following decades, this logo found its way into the paintings of Edward Manet, and at least 40 paintings by Picasso, and appeared in Ulysses' novel and a children's book. By 1871, the emblem was found even in the most arched corners of the British Empire, from the frozen Falkland coasts to the tropical shores of Mauritius. It is the oldest registered trademark in the UK. But the recognition of this slogan these days is not done as quickly as before. The Bass Bell logo joins other famous brands, such as Tea Twings, Levi Strauss, Peugeot, Johnson & Johnson, Heinz and Shell Oil, over 100 years of age.

Creative design tricks that stimulate creativity

The design of these mythological logos differs from other designs that emerged later and were widely criticized, as when Gap added a new square to its old logo. The company's most recent customer was a fuss that ended with the unveiling of the logo just one week after its appearance, or when the Royal Mail Service abandoned its 350-year heritage and took on a new logo and a new brand called 'Consignia'. The new logo and name, however, caused a great deal of confusion among the public, costing £ 2 million, and the rapidly designed company retreated. 'It's wonderful that people are passionate about certain brands,' says Allison Shields, assistant marketing professor at Ithaca College in New York. What makes a certain logo a mindset, as a kind of image that permeates the public consciousness, and enjoys respect and quality, or a sense of nostalgia? What makes other slogans disappear?
